value.overview: The White-breasted Wood-Wren (Henicorhina leucosticta) is a small, active wren of humid Neotropical forests. It usually stays close to the ground, where its rich brown back, barred wings, short tail, and contrasting white breast help identify it. Although often difficult to see in dense vegetation, it is readily detected by its loud, varied song and sharp calls. In Costa Rica, it is a familiar resident of suitable lowland and foothill forest, especially on the Caribbean side.
value.classification: The White-breasted Wood-Wren belongs to the wren family, Troglodytidae, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Henicorhina leucosticta. Several geographic forms are recognized across its broad range.
value.identification: This compact wren is about 10 cm long. Adults have warm chestnut-brown upperparts, a darker crown, a pale eyebrow, and black-and-white streaking on the sides of the head and neck. The throat and breast are white, becoming buff or grayish toward the belly, while the flanks are rufous. The wings and very short tail are barred dark and pale. It is distinguished from the similar Gray-breasted Wood-Wren by its whiter breast and generally lower-elevation distribution.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern South America. It inhabits humid evergreen forest, rainforest edges, dense secondary growth, ravines, tangled understory, and shaded plantations, usually near the ground. In Costa Rica it is a common resident of lowlands and lower foothills, particularly on the Caribbean slope, occurring to about 900 m in the north and about 1,200 m in the southeast. It can also occur locally in suitable humid forest on other slopes.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout most of its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Individuals may make short local movements in response to food, breeding, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in humid forest and dense understory. The pair builds a concealed, rounded or domed nest from plant fibers, leaves, and other vegetation, often in a bank, cavity, root mass, or dense low growth. The nest has a small entrance and is positioned close to the ground. Clutches commonly contain about two eggs. Both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young, while incubation and nestling details can vary among populations.
value.dietFeeding: The White-breasted Wood-Wren feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, ants, spiders, and similar forest-floor prey. It searches methodically through leaf litter, fallen branches, moss, roots, and low vegetation, frequently hopping between cover and flicking through debris. Its short wings and compact body suit movement through dense understory rather than prolonged flight. It may occasionally take small items from vegetation above ground level.
value.behavior: This wren is secretive, energetic, and strongly territorial. It usually forages in pairs or family groups and remains under dense cover, often moving with quick hops and short flights. Its loud song may be given repeatedly from a hidden perch and is frequently the easiest way to locate it. Pairs defend territories with songs and calls, and neighboring birds may respond in coordinated vocal exchanges. It is most active during daylight, especially in the morning.

conservation.populationTrend: Generally stable at the global level, with no strong evidence of a major overall decline.
